questions.q: What is the actual name of this capstone's fact table, and what is its grain?
options: dw.FactWorkOrder, with one row per work order
dw.FactSales, with one row per sales order line
stg.WorkOrder, with one row per production operation
dw.FactProduct, with one row per product
questions.explain: dw.FactWorkOrder is the fact table this architecture builds, and its grain is one row per work order — every column added to it has to be true at that grain.

questions.q: Why is dw.FactWorkOrder classified as an accumulating snapshot fact rather than a transaction fact?
options: Because StockedQty and ScrappedQty update on the same row as production progresses, instead of a new row being inserted at each step
Because it only ever holds one row total
Because it has no measures at all
Because it is refreshed only once a year
questions.explain: A transaction fact captures an event once and never changes. This fact's measures get revisited and updated as the work order moves through its lifecycle, which is the defining trait of an accumulating snapshot.

questions.q: Why does dw.FactWorkOrder have three foreign keys — StartDateKey, EndDateKey, and DueDateKey — all pointing at the same dw.DimDate table?
options: DimDate is a role-playing dimension here: one physical table referenced multiple times, each key representing a different role, instead of building three separate date dimensions
Because SQL Server requires at least three foreign keys per fact table
Because each date actually comes from a different, unrelated date dimension
It's a mistake in the design that should be fixed by removing two of the keys
questions.explain: Building three separate date dimensions would triple the maintenance cost of a table that never changes shape. A role-playing dimension lets one DimDate table serve all three roles.

questions.q: Why is Production.Location explicitly left out of this capstone's dimensional model?
options: It lives at the WorkOrderRouting (operation) grain, one level finer than the work-order grain this capstone chose, so modeling it would fan the fact table out past its intended grain
Because AdventureWorks2012 doesn't actually contain a Production.Location table
Because location data is never useful in a manufacturing model
Because it was already used by Data Modeling & Data Warehousing's capstone
questions.explain: A single work order can pass through several locations during production. Including it would either break the chosen grain or force an arbitrary rule — so this architecture scopes it out deliberately.

questions.q: How do the SSRS report and the Power BI dashboard in this architecture relate to each other?
options: They connect independently to the same dw.FactWorkOrder and dimension tables — neither tool feeds the other
Power BI reads its data from the SSRS report's output
SSRS reads its data from a Power BI dataset
They both read directly from Production.WorkOrder, bypassing the warehouse entirely
questions.explain: Both WorkOrderProductionSummary.rdl and the Power BI report are independent consumers of the same shared warehouse tables — that's the whole point of building a shared warehouse instead of two separate pipelines.
